name: Systems and Monitoring Reaction Rate
what: This subtopic covers the difference between open and closed systems and how the system type affects a reaction. It also explores different methods for measuring the rate of a chemical reaction over time.
why: Understanding systems is essential for interpreting experimental data and designing investigations. Knowing how to measure reaction rate underpins all experimental work in kinetics.

items.title: I can differentiate between open and closed systems
items.what: An open system allows both energy and matter to transfer between the reaction and its surroundings. A closed system allows energy transfer but not matter.
items.why: The type of system determines which measurement methods are valid and how the reaction behaves over time.
items.example: A flask with a loose top is an open system — gas can escape. A flask with a tightly sealed stopper is a closed system — gases produced are trapped inside.

items.title: I can outline how reactions proceed differently in open and closed systems
items.what: In an open system, gaseous products escape to the surroundings and cannot re-react. In a closed system, all reactants and products remain within the reaction vessel.
items.why: The system type affects whether concentration of products builds up, which in turn influences the rate and extent of the reaction.
items.example: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid in an open flask releases hydrogen gas into the air. In a sealed flask, the hydrogen gas accumulates inside the vessel.

items.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in concentration over time
items.what: Reaction rate can be measured by tracking how the concentration of a reactant decreases or how the concentration of a product increases over time.
items.why: Measuring concentration over time gives a direct indication of how fast reactants are being consumed and products are being formed.
items.example: In the reaction of sodium ions with phosphate ions, measuring the decrease in sodium ion concentration (mol/L) at regular time intervals allows the rate to be calculated.

items.title: I can describe how the rate of a reaction can be monitored by measuring changes in gas volume or mass over time
items.what: If a reaction produces a gas, the volume of gas collected can be measured over time. In an open system, the loss of mass as gas escapes can also be measured.
items.why: Concentration is not always practical to measure directly. Volume and mass are often easier to record with standard lab equipment.
items.example: In the reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, carbon dioxide gas is produced. Placing the flask on a balance and recording the decrease in mass every 60 seconds gives a measure of reaction rate.

items.title: I can express reaction rate mathematically using change in concentration divided by change in time
items.what: Reaction rate is calculated as the change in concentration (Δc) divided by the change in time (Δt). Similar expressions apply when using mass or volume instead of concentration.
items.why: A mathematical definition allows rates to be compared quantitatively between different experiments and conditions.
items.example: If the concentration of a reactant drops from 0.80 mol/L to 0.50 mol/L over 30 seconds, the rate is (0.80 - 0.50) / 30 = 0.01 mol/L/s.
